Improbability is a noun. It means the quality or state of something being unlikely to happen or unlikely to be true. In simpler words, it's a way of naming "how unlikely something is."

Think of it this way: when something has a very small chance of happening, that "smallness of chance" has a name — and that name is improbability.
Building the Concept from the Ground Up

To truly understand improbability, it helps to understand the word it comes from.

Probability is the likelihood of something happening. When you say something is probable, you mean it is likely — there's a good chance it will happen or be true. "Rain is probable tomorrow" means tomorrow will probably be rainy.

Now, improbable simply flips this. The prefix im- means "not," so improbable means not likely. "Rain is improbable tomorrow" means tomorrow will probably not be rainy.

Improbability, then, is the noun form of improbable. Instead of describing something (as the adjective improbable does), improbability names the quality itself — the state of being unlikely. It lets you talk about the unlikelihood as a thing in its own right.

For example: instead of saying "it is improbable that two people share the same fingerprint," you can say "the improbability of two people sharing the same fingerprint is enormous." Same idea, but now you are treating the unlikelihood as a concept you can hold, measure, and discuss.
The Most Important Distinction: Improbability ≠ Impossibility

This is the sharpest and most essential point about this word.

Impossible means something cannot happen — zero chance, full stop. A square circle is impossible. You cannot have one.

Improbable means something can happen, but the chances are very small. It is not ruled out — it is just very, very unlikely.

So improbability always lives in the space between "it might happen" and "it cannot happen." However slim the odds, if there is still a chance — even a tiny one — you are talking about improbability, not impossibility.

This is why we say things like "against all improbability, he survived" — meaning: the odds were stacked against him, a good outcome seemed nearly impossible, but it still happened because it was never truly impossible, just deeply unlikely.

If something were truly impossible, it could never happen at all — and there would be nothing to be surprised about.

Improbability is not one-size-fits-all. It exists on a sliding scale.

Something can have slight improbability — meaning it's a little unlikely, but not shocking. "Given that she rarely plays chess, winning one game has a slight improbability to it."

Something can have high improbability — meaning it's very unlikely, and you'd be genuinely surprised if it happened. "The improbability of guessing someone's 10-digit phone number correctly on the first try is enormous."

And something can have near-total improbability — meaning it's so close to impossible that it borders on miraculous if it occurs, yet it still theoretically can. "Scientists once calculated the improbability of life forming from random chemicals as being astronomically high — yet here we are."

The word itself doesn't tell you how improbable something is. Context and the words around it do that job. Improbability simply tells you: this thing sits on the unlikely end of the scale.
How It Feels in a Sentence

The most natural way to use improbability is with the word "of" following it, because you are usually naming what is improbable.

"The improbability of winning the lottery doesn't stop millions of people from buying tickets."
Here, "the improbability" = the very low likelihood of winning.

"Despite the improbability of it all, the two old friends ran into each other in a city of ten million people."
Here, it signals that the event was highly unlikely — which is exactly why it feels remarkable.

"Statisticians calculated the improbability of the same person being struck by lightning three times."
Here, improbability is being treated almost like a measurable quantity, something you can study and calculate.

You will often see phrases like "the sheer improbability" (emphasising just how unlikely something is), "despite the improbability" (used when something unlikely happened anyway), and "given the improbability" (used when reasoning about whether to expect something).

Beyond its technical meaning, improbability often carries a sense of wonder, surprise, or disbelief. When writers or speakers use it, they are frequently drawing your attention to something that shouldn't have happened — and yet somehow did, or might. It invites you to pause and appreciate the strangeness or rarity of a thing.

"The improbability of their love story made it all the more beautiful." — Here, the very fact that it was so unlikely to happen is what makes it feel special.

This emotional quality is part of why the word appears so often in literature, philosophy, and science — anywhere people are grappling with the odds of things, the fragility of outcomes, or the mystery of how the world unfolds.

Improbability (noun) is the quality or state of being unlikely. It names "how unlikely something is" as a concept you can discuss, measure, or reflect on. It is not the same as impossibility — improbable things can and do happen, they are simply not expected to. It exists on a scale, and the stronger the improbability, the more surprising it is when that thing occurs. The word often carries a tone of wonder, and is used whenever someone wants to acknowledge that the odds were against something — whether in science, everyday life, storytelling, or philosophy.
